newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Gunfire breaks out in Cambodian capital.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire breaks out in Cambodian capital.

text.p: Heavy gunfire broke out in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh on Tuesday night, apparently involving factions loyal to feuding co-prime ministers Hun Sen and Prince Norodom Ranariddh, witnesses said.

U.S. Ambassador Kenneth Quinn said a mortar round crashed into the front yard of his residence, shattering its windows, and a correspondent for Agence France Presse news agency was shot and slightly wounded, according to his girlfriend.
Shooting broke out near the centre of the city at about 10:30 p.m. (1530 GMT) and involved automatic weapons, mortars, grenades and possible tank rounds, witnesses reported.

Diplomats told Reuters the clashes appeared to pit armed units answering to Hun Sen and Ranariddh and broke out after pro-Ranariddh fighters converged on the home of national police chief Hok Lundy, a member of Hun Sen's political party.
Reuters photographer Patrick de Noirmont, who was in Norodom Avenue, a main thoroughfare, said streets were virtually empty as residents took cover in their homes to avoid gunfire.
Police sirens wailed through the city and police were setting up roadblocks, de Noirmont reported.
The gunfire diminished towards midnight (1700 GMT) but it was not clear whether the fighting had ended.
A government official reported two unidentified tanks moving up a main road from the south towards the capital.
Monitored radio transmissions by the two factions indicated that Hun Sen's side had ordered tanks and multiple rocket launchers into the area where most of the shooting had occurred.
The U.S. Embassy ordered all American citizens to stay in their homes until further notice.

Hun Sen and Ranariddh have been feuding for more than a year over power-sharing and how to best deal with the Maoist Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, now split into factions with its reviled strongman Pol Pot on the run.

Pol Pot, mastermind of the Khmer Rouge's genocidal "killing fields" rule of Cambodia in 1975-79, was reported fleeing toward Thailand with a handful of followers, holding several senior guerrillas, following thousands of defections in the guerrilla movement over the past 10 months.

Police chief Hok Lundy told Reuters in a telephone interview that he had been threatened by Ranariddh over the previous 24 hours. A Reuters news team tried to get to the house but were told by soldiers that it was too dangerous.
Witnesses said Ranariddh's men pointed B-40 rocket launchers at the house and Hok Lundy's bodyguards then started firing warning shots into the air.
Ranariddh's men then fired towards the house, on a major boulevard in downtown Phnom Penh, witnesses said. Much of the late-night gunfire was concentrated near the house.
There were no immediate reports of casualties, aside from the injury to the AFP journalist.
"(Hun Sen) is very angry this thing has happened and he will be taking punitive action," said a diplomat who holed up at a hotel overnight to escape the shooting near his home.

Diplomats, asked what provoked the clashes, told of a unspecified standoff at Hok Lundy's home on Monday night that ended with pro-Ranariddh troops leaving without incident. But they returned on Tuesday night and fighting resulted, they said.

Radio stations loyal to Ranariddh and Hun Sen attacked each other on the airways on Tuesday night. Pro-Ranariddh radio said many of Hun Sen's own military police and bodyguards had come out to do battle.
Hun Sen's Cambodian Peoples Party radio said: "Their side has come out so we must be ready."
Ranariddh and Hun Sen had been heading for confrontation for some time but their disputes apparently came to a head over the government's response to the flight of Pol Pot.
Ranariddh said on Tuesday Cambodia should capture Pol Pot to stand trial before a world tribunal.
Khieu Samphan, president of the Khmer Rouge's provisional government for years, recently announced he wanted to form a political alliance with Ranariddh.

Hun Sen, who was with the Vietnamese invasion force that eventually overthrew the Khmer Rouge regime and who formed an uneasy alliance with Ranariddh after U.N.-backed elections in 1993, has criticised Ranariddh for holding talks with Khieu Samphan and said that negotiating with the guerrillas was illegal.
